INTRODUCTION
1. This is an appeal by Agiliss Ltd (the Appellant), against an interlocutory Ruling of
19 January 2021 by the First Instance Division (FID) dismissing its Application to set aside
an earlier Ruling which allowed the Mauritius Oil Refineries Ltd, another Mauritian
company (the Intervener), to intervene in a Reference brought by the above-named
Appellant in the FID. The Reference is with respect to the imposition of duties and taxes on
edible oils imported from Egypt as a safeguard measure by the Government of the Republic
of Mauritius (the Respondent).
BACKGROUND
2. The Appellant, an importer of edible oils from the Republic of Egypt into the
Republic of Mauritius, instituted a Reference (the "Reference"), on 22 February 2019 before
the FID under Article 26 of the COMESA (the Treaty) challenging the introduction of
additional tax on edible oils from Egypt and for the determination by the CCJ of the legality
of the newly introduced duty.
3. By Notice of Motion dated 6 August 2019 (Application No. 2 of 2019), the
Intervener, an local manufacturer of edible oils, sought leave to intervene in the Reference
to support the imposition of the additional tax by the Respondent (the Application for
Intervention). The Appellant objected to the Application for Intervention and filed its reply
on 6 August 2020 in accordance with Rule 50(2) of the COM ESA Court of Justice Rules of
Procedure 2016 (the Rules).
4. The Application for Intervention was heard on 8 January 2020 by the FID before a
bench of seven Honourable Judges including Honourable Justice Georges. The FID gave its
Ruling on 14 Januaiy 2020 (the "Intervention Ruling") whereby it granted leave to the
Intervener to intervene in the Reference.
1
FF1199

FF2200
4121573a81ae4e1dac99d3cf2921748b-4
5. By Notification dated 31 January 2020, the Honourable Principal Judge directed the
Intervener to file its statement of intervention (the "Statement of Intervention") within 15
days of the date of the Notification. By Notification dated 14 February 2020, the Honourable
Principal Judge issued directions granting a request from the Intervener for an extension of
time to file its Statement oflntervention until 29 February 2020.
6. Two weeks after the hearing of the Intervention proceedings, it came to the attention
of the Appellant that Honourable Justice Georges was acquainted with the Intervener
inasmuch as he knew the CEO and Counsel for the Intervener. By letter dated 27 February
2020, the Appellant requested the recusal of Honourable Mr Justice Georges from the
proceedings in connection with the Reference under Rule 9( 6) of the Rules on the basis that
the impartiality of Honourable Justice Georges may reasonably be questioned.
7. By letter dated 6 March 2020, the Intervener admitted that 'though acquainted to
with Hon. Mr Justice Georges, the Intervener's CEO or Counsel have no close proximity
with his Lordship' and prayed that the request of the Appellant for the recusal of
Honourable Mr Justice Georges be dismissed.
8. The parties were, by Notification of the FID in a letter dated 11 March 2020, given
notice of the recusal of Honourable Justice Georges sua sponte 'on the principle that the
Court should at all times be above criticism from any perception of bias and that the
decision is by no means an admission of the issues raised in the request'.
9. By letter dated 25 March 2020, the Appellant requested that the Application for
Intervention be heard anew before a reconstituted bench, which request was objected to by
the Intervener by letter dated 28 April 2020.
10. The Appellant made various requests to the Court for extensions of time to file its
reply to the Intervener's Statement of Intervention including on the basis of difficulties
caused by the COVID-19 pandemic. By letter dated 4 May 2020, the Appellant also
appealed to the Court for time to file a substantive application requesting the setting aside of
the Intervention Ruling.
2
FF2200

FF2211
4121573a81ae4e1dac99d3cf2921748b-5
11. Subsequent to the Honourable Principal Judge suspending the filing of all processes
by all parties due to the difficulties caused by the COVID-19 pandemic by Notification
dated 8 May 2020, by further Notification dated 21 July 2020, the Honourable Principal
Judge directed the Appellant to file its application for hearing anew of the Application for
Intervention and its reply to the Statement of Intervention by 6 August 2020.
12. By Notice of Motion dated 6 August 2020, the Appellant filed its application for
hearing anew together with its supporting affidavit (the "Application for Hearing Anew").
On the same date the Appellant filed its reply to the Statement of Intervention together with
its annexures.
13. Ultimately, on 19 January 2021, the FID delivered its ruling after hearing the parties
whereby it dismissed the Application for Hearing Anew.
14. By that decision, the FID held that:
1. It had no jurisdiction to set aside its own intervention Ruling as the Treaty
and the Rules have no governing provisions confering on it such jurisdiction.
11. The challenge to the participation of Justice Georges in the intervention
hearing on the ground of the perception of bias was not substantiated as the
Appellant failed to adduce evidence that the Judge had a close relationship
with the CEO and Counsel of the Intervener.
iii. Even though the Application to set aside the Intervention Ruling was brought
under Rule 41 of the Rules, it was late in terms of Rule 43 of the Rules and as
such was inegular and incompetent.
15. The Appellant now appeals against the dismissal of its Application.
3
FF2211

FF2222
4121573a81ae4e1dac99d3cf2921748b-6
GROUNDS OF APPEAL
16. The Appeal is on the following grounds -
the First Instance Division erred in law and in fact in holding that the Appellant
1.
failed to discharge the burden of proof of the extent of the relationship which could
have led to the alleged bias;
the First Instance Division erred in law and in fact in failing to hold that the recusa1
11.
of Justice Bernard Georges (Justice Georges) gave rise to a perception of bias;
m. The First Instance Division failed to give due weight and consideration to the
obligations under Article 22(4) of the COMESA Treaty and Rule 9(5) of the
COMESA Rules of Court on Justice Georges to disclose his acquaintanceship with
the Intervener's Chief Executive Officer (CEO) and Counsel and recuse himself
prior to the hearing of Application No. 1 of 2020; and the recusal of Justice Georges
sua sponte upon the request of the Appellant in determining Application No. 1 of
2020;
1v. the First Instance Division erred in law and in fact in holding that the Appellant
should hold its peace on the alleged perception of bias on the part of Justice Georges
on the basis that the Appellant had failed to act with promptitude in seeking the
recusal of Justice Georges;
v. the First Instance Division erred in law and in fact in holding that the Ruling of 19
January 2021 in Application No. 1 of 2020 need not be disturbed because Justice
Georges' participation in Application No. 1 of2020 was mere surplusage;
vi. the First Instance Division erred in law and in fact in holding that Application No. I
of 2020 is incompetent and procedurally irregular;
vii. the First Instance Division erred in law and in fact in holding that it did not have
jurisdiction under the COMESA Treaty and the COMESA Rules of Court to
determine Application No. 1 of 2020; and
4 /<

~-
FF2222

FF2233
4121573a81ae4e1dac99d3cf2921748b-7
v111. the First Instance Division failed to set aside the Ruling of 19 January 2021 in
Application No. 1 of 2020; and the First Instance Division failed to order the
rehearing of Application No. 2 of 2019.
17 . The Appellant seeks the following reliefs -
that the Ruling of 19 January 2021 in Application No.1 of 2020 be set aside;
1.
that the Application of the Intervener by Notice of Motion dated 6 August 2019
11.
bearing reference Application No.2 of 2019 for leave to intervene in the case bearing
Reference No.I of 2019 before the First Instance Division of the COME SA Court of
Justice(CCJ) be heard anew;
that the proceedings in Reference No. I of 2019 be stayed pending the determination
111.
of the present Appeal;
1v. that the costs in this Appeal and in Application No. 1 of 2020 before the FID abide
the result of this Appeal; and
v. such other Orders as the Court may direct.
PRELIMINARIES
18. Before outlining the main issues to be decided in the Appeal, we will address
preliminary issues raised by the Respondent, co-Respondents and Intervener. These are that:
The Appellant has no locus standi to prosecute the Reference in the FID and this
1.
Appeal as it has not exhausted domestic remedies in the Republic of Mauritius
before coming to the COMESA Court of Justice(CCJ). As such, the Reference
should be permanently stayed to compel the Appellant to go back and exhaust
domestic remedies in the Republic of Mauritius first;
FF2233

FF2244
4121573a81ae4e1dac99d3cf2921748b-8
ii. The FID ruling appealed against is an interlocutory ruling and not appealable; and
lll. The 1st and 2nd Co-Respondents should be struck out being unnecessary parties.
(i) Locus Standi: Exhaustion of Local Remedies
19. The Respondent, Co-Respondents Nos. 3 and 4 and the Intervener have raised the
objection that the Appellant has failed to exhaust local remedies as required by Article 26 of
the Treaty before resorting to the CCJ. Without having instituted proceedings in the courts
of Mauritius, a reference was filed in the CCJ.
20. In response, the Appellant submits that there are no local remedies available in
Mauritius, the Supreme Court of Mauritius having decided in Polytol Paints & Adhesive
Manufacturers Co Ltd v The Minister of Finance [2009J SCJ 106 that they have no
jurisdiction to apply the Treaty, it not having been domesticated in that country.
21. The Appellant further submits that the defence of the Respondent, Co-Respondents
Nos. 3 and 4 and the Intervener relating to locus standi is not receivable in this present
matter as it runs foul of Rule 96(2) of the Rules in that it changes the subject matter of the
Appeal and instead seeks to determine the Reference. Thus, the defence ought not be
entertained in these proceedings but is to be addressed before the FID in the main
proceedings in the Reference.
22. We have taken into consideration submissions by all parties and we hold as follows:
23. We take judicial notice that from the record in the FID, the issue of locus standi was
raised. However, this issue has not yet been resolved as the FID did not rule on it, having
been preoccupied with intervention, setting aside and trial anew proceedings. Nevertheless,
that does not give this Court the power to usurp the jurisdiction of the FID. We do not agree
with the characterisation of the Respondent that the fact that Article 7 of the Treaty provides
for the establishment of the Court of Justice as one of the eight Organs of the Common
Market means that the FID and Appellate Division are one court so that challenges of locus
standi can be brought either to the FID or the Appellate Division.
6
FF2244

FF2255
4121573a81ae4e1dac99d3cf2921748b-9
24. It is important to note that Article 7 of the Treaty is further qualified by Article 23
which provides as follows:
'General Jurisdiction oft he Court
The Court shall have jurisdiction to adjudicate upon all matters which may be
referred to it pursuant to the Treaty.
The First instance Division of the Court shall have the jurisdiction to hear and
determine at first instance, subject to right ofa ppeal to the Appellate Division under
paragraph 2, any matter brought before the Court in accordance with the Treaty.
Appeal shall lie to the Appellate Division on points of law; grounds of lack of
jurisdiction; or procedural irregularity'.
25. It therefore follows that, subject to the jurisdiction of the Appellate Division to
provide advisory opinions under Article 32 of the Treaty and preliminary rulings under
Article 30 of the Treaty, the Apellate Division has no original jurisdiction and matters can
come to the Appellate Division by way of appeal only.
26. It is also noteworthy that apart from raising the issue of exhaustion of local remedies
in their submissions, the Respondent, Co-Respondents Nos. 3 and 4 and Intervener did not
file a cross appeal with respect to this line of argument. lnfact, they could not as the FID had
not made a determination on the issue.
27. We therefore dismiss the preliminary objection raised by the Respondent, 3rd and 4th
Co-Respondents and Intervener that the Appellant did not exhaust domestic remedies in the
Republic of Mauritius.
(ii) Appeal against Interlocutory Rulings
28. The Respondent and Co-Respondents 3 and 4 submit that:
the Appeal is misconceived as in so far as it is made against a Ruling on the
1.
FID which is not final.
7
FF2255

FF2266
4121573a81ae4e1dac99d3cf2921748b-10
in the spirit of the Treaty, the jurisdiction of the Appellate Court, has been
11.
limited to the taking up of appeals only against a final decision of the FID.
111. this conclusion comes out from a reading of Article 23 of the Treaty which
provides that appeals can only lie from a decision of the FID to the Appellate
Division on points of law, grounds of lack of jurisdiction, or procedural
irregularity.
29. None of the other parties to this Appeal addressed the Court on this point.
30. Having carefully considered the issue, we hold that the Appeal is admissible as it is
on points of law, jurisdiction, and irregularity.
31. The fact that the Ruling appealed against is merely interlocutory does not remove the
right of a party to approach the Appellate Division for relief In the Government of the
Republic of Malawi v Malawi Mobile case, the Court allowed an appeal on the ground of
lack ofj urisdiction against a decision of the FID which was not final.
32. We therefore dismiss this preliminary objection.
(iii) Striking out the pt and 2nd Respondents as Wrongly Sued.
33. Counsel for the 151 and 2nd Respondents submitted that the 1st and 2nd Repondents
have been wrongly joined to this action, being mere custodians of the Treaty and not
involved in the activities the subject matter of the Reference in the FID. As such, he prays
that they be struck out. Further, the I st and 2nd Respondents are only relevant in the
Reference but not the Appeal.
34. We hold that, just like the issue of locus standi in the sense of exhaustion of local
remedies, the FID has not dealt with this matter. Apart from raising the issue in submissions,
the !51 and 2nd Respondents have not filed a cross appeal with respect thereto. Obviously,
there could be no cross appeal as there has been no determination of this issue by the FID.
8
FF2266

FF2277
4121573a81ae4e1dac99d3cf2921748b-11
35. As already stated earlier on in this Ruling, matters come before the Appellate
Division by way of appeal, not in the first instance. As such, it would be premature for us to
express ourselves on this issue. The matter needs to be first ventilated before the FID level.
36. For these reasons, we dismiss this preliminary prayer.
MAIN ISSUES
37. The main issues for the determination in this Appeal are:
(a) Whether or not there is a procedural irregularity in the Application to Set
aside the Intervention Ruling.
(b) Whether or not the FID has jurisdiction to entertain an application to set aside
its own intervention ruling.
(c) Whether or not there is an inference of bias on the part of Justice Georges.
(d) Whether or not the Intervention Ruling must be set aside because of the
participation of Justice Georges.
(e) Whether or not there is procedural irregularity in the Application to Set aside
the Intervention Ruling.
Issue (a) - Whether or not there is a procedural irregularity in the application to set
aside the Intervention Ruling.
38. The FID held that Application No. l of 2020 was incompetent and procedurally
in-egular, the Appellant having failed to file the Application for Hearing Anew within 30
days as provided under Rule 43(2) of the Rules. The Appellant also failed to serve the
Application for Hearing Anew on all parties within 15 days as required under Rule 41 (9) of
the Rules.
9
FF2277

FF2288
4121573a81ae4e1dac99d3cf2921748b-12
Appellant's Submissions
39. The Appellant submitted that:
the Application for Hearing Anew was rightly made under Rule 41 of the
1.
Court Rules and not under Rule 43 of the Court Rules as erroneously held by
the FID. Rule 41 does not prescribe any time limit to initiate interlocutory
applications.
Rule 43 of the Rules only applies to the setting aside of ex parte orders or ex
11.
parte judgments. Such applications are to be made within 30 days from the
date of service of the ex parte order or ex parte judgment. This argument is
buttressed by the provisions of Rule 43(2) of the Rules requiring service of
the ex parte orders or judgments, clearly indicating that Rule 43 of the Rules
applies only to ex parte orders or ex parte judgments. In the present case, the
Intervention Ruling which was being challenged was made inter partes, such
that it falls outside the purview of Rule 43 of the Rules and was instead
brought under Rule 41.
iii. The decision of the FID in the case of Eastern and Southern African Trade
and Development Bank (PTA ) and Dr Michael Gondwe v Martin Ogang
Reference/ B/2000 supports the proposition that an application to set aside a
ruling is to be made under the generic rule providing for interlocutory
applications. In that case, the application was made under the then Rule 82 of
the Court Rules which reads as a generic rule for interlocutory applications
and corresponds to the present Rule 41.
1v. As far as the Appellant's alleged failure to serve the application for hearing
anew within 15 days as required under Rule 41 (9) of the Rules, the
requirement was waived by the Principal Judge by virtue of a notification
dated 21 July 2020 where she directed that the Applicant shall file an
Application for Hearing Anew of the Application for Intervention by
MOROIL Ltd on or before 6 August 2020 and the Respondent, Co-
10
~ ~ FF2288

FF2299
4121573a81ae4e1dac99d3cf2921748b-13
Respondents and Intervener shall file their responses to the Application for
Hearing Anew of the Application for Intervention within fifteen (15) days of
the date of filing of the Application for Hearing Anew of the Application for
Intervention.
v. Since all filings in the Reference were made on the FID's electronical
system, the Principal Judge waived the requirement for service of the
Application for Hearing Anew.
v1. In the alternative, compliance with rules of procedure ought not to be applied
so strictly as to defeat the ends of justice. Rule 3 of the Rules provides that
the CCJ has broad jurisdiction to administer substantive justice. More
specifically, Rule 3(1) expressly provides that the inherent power of the
Court shall not be limited or otherwise affected by the Rules.
v11. No prejudice whatsoever was caused to the Respondent, the Co-Respondents
and Intervener as a result of the Appellant's alleged failure to serve the
Application for Hearing Anew on them inasmuch as they were given an
opportunity to file their responses, written submissions and addressed the
Court in extenso during the sitting of 13 January 2021 when the Application
for Hearing Anew was heard.
v111. Therefore, the Application for Hearing Anew was not procedurally irregular
and complied with the requirements of the Rules and/or the directions issued
by the Principal Judge.
Respondent and Co-Respondents 3 and 4 Submissions
40. Counsel for the Respondent and Co-Respondents Nos. 3 and 4 did not submit directly
on this issue.
Intervener's Submissions
41. The Intervener submitted as follows:
11
ffe
FF2299

FF3300
4121573a81ae4e1dac99d3cf2921748b-14
i. The Appellant is guilty of abuse of process as this is not the first procedural error
by them as earlier in the FID, they tried to move the Court by letter instead of an
application.
The submssions of the Respondent and Co-Respondents Nos. 3 and 4 are fully
11.
supported.
The Application for recusal of Justice Georges in the FID came late, six weeks
111.
after discovery of the acqaintance between Justice Georges and the CEO and
Counsel of the Intervener.
Discussions and Analysis
42. The FID held that in their view, the Appellant erred to argue that if a wrong rule was
invoked to file its Application to Set aside the Court's Intervention Ruling on account of an
alleged perception of bias on the part of Justice Georges by virtue of his acquaintance with
the CEO and Counsel for the Intervener, Rule 3 of the Rules was available to them to correct
the deficiency.
43. The Court stated that procedures that are provided under the Rules are to regulate the
conduct of business of the Court and they can hardly be said to be technicalities. In answer
to the question whether Rule 3(1) of the Rules could cure perceived defects with the
Appellant's Application in the FID, the Court relied on the Supreme Court of Kenya
decision in the case of Moses Mwicigi & 14 Others v Independent Electoral and Boundaries
Commission & 5 Others [2016) eKLR, particularly paragraph 66, to dismiss the Appellant's
application. In that case, the Supreme Cout stated:
"This Court has on a number ofo ccasions remarked upon the importance o_frules of
procedure, in the conduct of litigation. In many cases, procedure is so closely
intertwined with the substance of a case, that it befits not the attribute of mere
technicality. The conventional wisdom, indeed, is that procedure is the handmaiden
of justice. Where a procedural motion bears the very ingredients of just
12
{fr.
FF3300

FF3311
4121573a81ae4e1dac99d3cf2921748b-15
determ;nation, and yet it is overlooked by a litigant, the Court would not hesitate to
declare the attendant pleadings incompetent. "
44. We find that the issue of whether the Application was made under Rule 43 as
opposed to 41 is a matter of technicality of procedure not closely intertwined with the
substance of the case. Failure to observe such a technicality is curable by Rule 3(1) of the
Rules particularly where, as in this case, no prejudice was occasioned to the other parties
who were able to respond to the Application and be heard on the matter. This is the position
we took in Government of the Republic of Malavvi v Malawi Mobile Ltd, Appeal No. 1 of
2016 where failure to comply with technical rules of procedure on the requirement to file a
response within a specified time period by an appellant was cured by Rule 3(1) especially
when such failure was occasioned by ambiguity in our own rules.
45. We dare say in this Appeal as well that, failure by the Appellant to make a proper
filing was caused by a lacuna in our own Rules for not providing the procedural rule for
applications such as those in the repealed Rule 82 under which the Ogang case was filed.
Clearly, the Appellant should not be penalised for a lacuna in our Rules of Procedure.
46. Further, unlike the Mwicigi case, we hold the view that in the instant case, procedure
is not so intertwined with substance as to render injustice in case of lack of compliance
thereof. On the contrary, we find that strict adherence to procedure would cause injustice in
this case.
Issue (b) - Whether or not the FID has jurisdiction to entertain an application to set
aside its own intervention ruling.
Appellant's Submissions
4 7. The appellant submitted that the FID has jurisdiction to set aside its own intervention
ruling sourced from:
(i) Articles 23 of the Treaty which gives the Court jurisdiction to adjudicate upon
all matters that may be referred to it pursuant to the Treaty; and
13
FF3311

FF3322
4121573a81ae4e1dac99d3cf2921748b-16
(ii) Article 35 of the Treaty which gives it jurisdiction to make interim orders.
48. In support of the above submission, the Appellant placed reliance on the EACJ case
of Attorney General oft he Republic ofK enya and Prof Anyang' Nyon 'g & 10 others [A pp.
No. 5 of2 007.
Respondent, 3rd and 4th Co-Respondents' Submissions
49. On their part, the Respondent, 3rd and 4th Co-Respondents submitted that the FID
had no jurisdiction to set aside its Ruling of 14 January 2020 because it had no jurisdiction
to sit on appeal over its own decision.
Intervener's Submissions
50. The Intervener did not offer any submissions on this point.
Discussion and Analysis
51. The question before us is whether the FJD has jurisdiction to reopen the Intervention
Ruling on account of the alleged perception of bias on the part of Justice Georges.
52. It is therefore appropriate to set out first the relevant provision for the purposes of
the present Appeal.
53. The CCJ was established as an Organ of the Common Market under Article 7 of the
Treaty. Articles 19 and 23 (s upra paragraph 24) of the Treaty spell out the jurisdiction of the
CCJ. Article 19 provides as follows;
""Article 19
Establishment oft he Court
The Court of Justice established under Article 7 of this Treaty shall ensure the
14
FF3322

FF3333
4121573a81ae4e1dac99d3cf2921748b-17
adherence to law in the interpretation and application oft his Treaty. .... "
54. Additionally, Rule 3 of the Rules provides that :-
"Nothing in these Rules shall limit or otherwise affect the inherent power of the
Court to administer substantive justice without undue regard to technicalities, and to
preserve lhe dignity, or prevent abuse oft he process oft he Court".
55. We begin our determination of this issue by drawing attention to Sir Jack Jacob's
definition of inherent jurisdiction in H Jacob ··The Court's Inherent Jurisdiction" (1970) 23
CLP 23 where he defines it as a:-
''[. .. } residual source of powers, which the court may draw upon as necessary
whenever it is just or equitable to do so, in particular to ensure the observance oft he
due process of law, to prevent vexation or oppression, to do justice .......... The
juridical basis of this jurisdiction is therefore the authority of the judiciary to
uphold, lo protect and to fulfill the judicial function of administering justice
according lo law in a regular, orderly and effective manner. .,
56. Thus, inherent jurisdiction is a widely accepted concept m Common Law
jurisdictions. It is not disputed that the circumstances of its application may vary from one
legal system to another. Nevertheless, inherent jurisdiction remains a fundamental principle
in all judicial systems including the CCJ.
57. In Anton Piller KG v Manufacturing Processes Ltd [1976] Ch 55 (CA), the English
Court of Appeal established its inherent jurisdiction to grant an ex parte order to a party to
enter, search and remove property from the premises of its opponent in civil litigation when
it is likely that the opponent was going to destroy integral evidence.
58. Similarly, the Supreme Court of Canada held in Re Sproule (1886) 12 SCR J..10 at
180, cited in Charles, above n 41, 121- 122 that:-
15
FF3333

FF3344
4121573a81ae4e1dac99d3cf2921748b-18
··every superior court [ . .] has incident to its jurisdiction an inherent right to inquire
into andj udge the regularity or abuse ofi ts process. "
59. On the international level, the application of this principle was recognised in
Prosecutor v. Duskotadic, IT-94-l-A-R77 where the International Tribunal of the Former
Yugoslavia, stated in its judgment that it possessed inherent jurisdiction in the following
words:
"There is no mention in the Tribunal's Statute ofi ts power to deal with contempt. The
Tribunal does, however, possess an inherent jurisdiction, deriving from its judicial
junction, to ensure that its exercise of the jurisdiction ·which is expressly given lo it
by that Statute is not frustrated and that its basic judicial functions are
safeguarded."
60. In the Northern Cameroons and Nuclear Tests cases 1963 1. CJ 15, 29 (Dec. 2), the
International Court of Justice (ICJ) explained that its inherent jurisdiction is the basis of
certain powers it exercises and principles and rules of international law it applies. In this
case the court stated:
"There are inherent limitations on the exercise of the judicial function which the
Court, as a court ofjustice, can never ignore ... Ift he Court is satis,fied, whatever the
nature oft he relief claimed, that to adjudicate the merits ofa n Application would be
inconsistent with its judicial.function, it should refuse to do so. "
6 I. The Court (ICJ) expanded on the scope and source of this jurisdiction in the Nuclear
Tests case as follows:
[l}t should be emphasized that the Court possesses an inherent jurisdiction enabling
it to take such action as may be required. ... to provide for the orderly sertlement of
all matters in dispute, to ensure the observance of the "inherent limitations on the
exercise of the judicial June/ion" of the Court, and to "mainlain ifs judicial

Lordship to refuse recusal and put forward argument to support his impartiality or to
disclose his interest thereby allowing the Appellant to decide whether to waive its objection.
117. Sitting as a judge in a Regional Court where it is not frequent occurrence that judges
discover an acquaintance, Justice Georges needed, in the light of Article 22 of the Treaty, to
disclose his acquaintance with the CEO and Counsel of the Intervener to the President, even
if no actual bias was perceived. It was up to the President to consider whether an appearance
of bias could arise. The failure to disclose and the self recusal which followed, is to be read
in favour of the Appellant.
118. For the above reasons, we find that the FID erred when it concluded that the nature
of the acquaintance between the Judge and the CEO and Counsel did not give rise to bias or
an apprehension of bias.

Discussion and Analysis
124. Having determined that the decision of Justice Georges to recuse himself has given
rise to a perception of impartiality in light of Article 22(4 ) of the Treaty and Rules 9(5) of
the Rules, the Court must now resolve whether the Intervention Ruling of 14 January 2020
must be set aside because of the participation of Justice Georges in the Application for
Intervention.
125. As already stated above, the inherent exceptional jurisdiction of collegiate courts to
vacate their own decisions on grounds of the breach of the fundamental principle ofj udicial
impartiality is widely settled in Common Law jurisdictions. What needs to be considered is
whether one member's disqualification is always a fatal contaminant. This is a fundamental
question.
34
FF5522

FF5533
4121573a81ae4e1dac99d3cf2921748b-37
126. In that context, we hold that a recusal application before a single judge normally
raises no question as to who the decision-maker should be, or how the decision ought to be
taken. The impugned judge would normaly be expected to decide the matter personally, and
an error would affect only that judge's decision.
127. We are of the view that a member of a court or tribunal sitting with others incorrectly
may well have the effect of fataly contaminating the ultimate decision of the Court. This
school of thought is widely recognised in most legal systems.
128. In Martin Ogang (Supra), this Court set aside the proceedings in which Justice
Ogoola participated on the ground of reasonable perception of bias.
129. More precisely, in Williams v .Pennsylvania (Supra), the Supreme Court of the
United States gave an important clarification on the effect that a disqualified judge may have
on the proceeding. It held as follow:-
" The Court has little trouble concluding that a due process violation arising from
the participation ofa n interested judge is a defect "not amenable., to harmless-error
review, regardless ofw hether the judge's vote was dispositive. .. The deliberations of
an appellate panel, as a general rule, are confidential. As a result, it ;s neither
possible nor productive to inquire whether the jurist in question might have
influenced the views of his or her colleagues during the decision making process.
Indeed, one purpose of judicial confidentiality is lo assure jurists that they can
reexamine old ideas and suggest new ones, while both seeking to persuade and being
open to persuasion by their colleagues. "
130. As Justice Brennan stated in Aetna Life Ins. Co. c. Lavoie, 475 US 813 (1986) in his
concurrence opinion:
"The descriplion ofa n opinion as being for the court· connotes more than merely
that the opinion has been joined by a majority oft he participating judges. It reflects
the fact that these judges have exchanged ideas and arguments in deciding the case.
35

FF5544
4121573a81ae4e1dac99d3cf2921748b-38
It re.fleets the collective process ofd eliberation which shapes the court's perceptions
of which issues must be addressed and, more importantly. how they must be
addressed. And, while the influence of any single participant in this process can
never be measured with precision, experience teaches us that each member's
involvement plays a part in shaping the court ·s ultimate disposition." 475 U S., at
831.
13 I. In light of the above, we hold that since the participation of Justice Georges in the
proceeding was an error that affected the FID's court adjudicatory process on the
Application for Intervention by the Intervener, the Appellant must be granted an opportunity
to present his claims to a Court unburdened by any perception of bias.
132. Therefore, we adopt the views of the Supreme Cou11 of the United States in Williams
v. Pennsylvania (Supra). that it would be impossible to measure how Justice Georges
participated and how he might have influenced the views of his colleagues during the
decision making process which is confidential, and by consequence, his self-disqualification
may well have the effect of fatally contaminating the ultimate decision of the FID.
133. Thus, we do not accept the FJD·s holding that Justice Georges's participation in the
intervention proceeding was surplusage. In fact, Justice Georges's participation in the
process can never be measured with precision, and this does not change because of the
assertion made by the FID that the ruling of 14 January 2020 was unanimous. It is crystal
clear that the assertion cannot lead this Court to accept that the disqualified judge's vote was
unnecessary.
134. Accordingly, we do not agree with what has been contented by learned Counsel for
the Intervener that the application to set aside a ruling on the basis of perceived bias of one
of seven judges was unreasonable, would unduly delay the hearing of the reference and that
in any event any resultant hearing anew will produce the same result.
135. In this regard we are fortified in our position by what the United States Supreme
Court held in Williams v. Pennsylvania (Supra) that:-

''The Commonwealth points out that ordering a rehearing before the Pennsylvania
Supreme Court may not provide complete relief to Williams because judges who
were exposed to a disqualified judge may still be influenced by their colleague's
views when they rehear the case. .. An inability to guarantee complete relieff or a
constitutional violation, however, does not justify withholding a remedy altogether.
Allowing an appellate panel to reconsider a case without the participation of the
interested member will permit judges to probe lines of analysis or engage in
discussions they may have felt constrained to avoid in their first deliberations"
136. In view of the forgoing, we hold that the Appellant was not accorded a fair trial in
the FID by the participation of Justice Georges in the intervention proceedings leading to the
Intervention Ruling of 14 January 2021.
137. The Intervention Ruling must therefore be set aside.

138. In view of our findings on the four main issues identified in this Ruling for the
Court's determination, we hold in the final analysis as follows:
The Ruling of the FID that it has no jurisdiction to set aside its Intervention Ruling,

that the Appellant failed to prove bias or appearance thereof on the part of Justice
Georges, and that the Appellant's application in the FID for setting aside was
incompetent and irregular is hereby reversed.
The Intervention Ruling of 14 January 2021 is hereby set aside.
